title: A seat at the king's table (2 Samuel 9)
hookLine: David looks for any of Saul's family to show kindness, and finds a lame grandson

lines: ANY LEFT OF THE HOUSE OF SAUL?
cards: "Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" That's the king's question. From a new king, a question about the old king's family could sound like a threat.
They find a servant of Saul's house named Ziba, and he answers. There is one: a son of Jonathan, living in a place called Lo-debar, in another man's house.
And Ziba adds one more detail, as if it might matter to the king: he is lame on his feet.

teach.b: His name is Mephibosheth. Earlier in the book we learn how he became lame: when he was five, news came that Saul and Jonathan had died, and his nurse snatched him up to flee, and in her hurry he fell.
Now he's grown, with a young son of his own, the grandson of the fallen king, and he's summoned to the palace. He falls on his face before David, and David's first words are: "Fear not."

Then the promise, in the King James Bible: "I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father's sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father; and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually."
Kindness, in Hebrew, is chesed: loyal love, the faithfulness that keeps a promise. David and Jonathan had sworn that their love would reach their children. Jonathan is gone.

teach.h: SUCH A DEAD DOG AS I AM.
teach.b: Mephibosheth can hardly take it in: "What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am?" That's how small he feels.

teach.h: AT THE TABLE, AND STILL LAME.
teach.b: And the chapter's last line puts two facts side by side, with no comment: he "did eat continually at the king's table; and was lame on both his feet." He is still lame. He still eats at the king's table.

The kindness doesn't erase his story; it gives it a place. Some Christians hear their own story here: brought in from far away, given a seat they didn't earn, for someone else's sake, a picture of grace.
Others simply hear a king keeping a promise to a dead friend.

how: Some Christians tell the story of Mephibosheth as a picture of grace and of keeping promises, and preachers use it to speak about welcoming people who have been left out.

o: Saul's general, who led his army against David
David's oldest son, who later rebelled against him
Jonathan's lame son, given a seat at David's table

games.q: the king's table — tap the pairs.

s: David was looking for Saul's family to remove a rival
he asked so that he could show kindness for Jonathan's sake.
Ziba says there is a son of Jonathan, lame on his feet.
at the king's table, Mephibosheth was healed
the last line says he ate at the king's table and was lame on both his feet.

games.q: you're David. you've found Jonathan's son, lame, living in another man's house in Lo-debar. he falls on his face before you. what do you give him?
o: a little money, and send him home.
Saul's land, and a seat at your table.
games.why: "Fear not," and then all the land of Saul, and bread at the king's table continually, for Jonathan's sake.

practice: Think of someone you've been at odds with, then look past them to the people around them: a child, a parent, a friend who had nothing to do with your quarrel.
Choose one, and picture what kindness to them would look like: a greeting, a small help, including them instead of avoiding them. If you pray, hold that person before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Mephibosheth. Jonathan's lame son, Saul's grandson, brought in by David and given a seat at the king's table as a promise of loyal love.

orig.note: Hebrew: loyal love, kindness. David shows chesed for Jonathan's sake (2 Samuel 9:1, 3, 7).

carryVoice: Your line: always at my table. A promise to a friend, kept for his son. See you tomorrow.
